666aeebed7:
This chapter follows a change to a prompt, a model, a retrieval index or a tool on its way from "the offline eval looks better" to "it is live for everyone, it is measurably better, and nothing that matters got worse".

It covers online experiments and their statistics, then shadow mode and canary. It sets out the order of questions to ask when quality regresses. It ranks the cost levers and latency levers by risk. And it builds the unit-economics model that tells you which of those levers are worth pulling.
eeb3ee54a2:
The exam facts quoted in this guide (63 items, 120 minutes, $175, seven domains with weights of 19, 17, 16, 14, 14, 13 and 7 percent) come from third-party summaries of the CCAR-P blueprint. Treat them as a study map. Verify them against the official exam guide before you book.

Every price, discount multiplier, speed, rate limit, latency and pass rate in this chapter is an illustrative planning number, chosen to make the arithmetic visible. Check the docs (pricing, prompt caching, batch processing, rate limits) for current values. Replace the placeholders with your own telemetry before you quote a figure to anyone.
6e6b192803:
The whole chapter fits in two sentences.

A change to an LLM system is a hypothesis about a metric, so it is tested on the smallest audience that can falsify it, with the primary metric, the guardrails, the sample size and the stopping rule written down before the data arrives, and it is judged per segment because the requirement is per segment.

When something is wrong, the cause is found by asking the cheapest discriminating question first (what changed, where, which component), and when something is expensive, the saving comes from the lever with the best saving per unit of risk, each lever measured against the segment thresholds and the latency SLA before it is kept.
4c8ef62fe3:
Everything else follows from those two sentences.

The rollout ladder exists so that risk grows only as evidence grows. Pre-registration exists so that nobody can pick the metric after seeing the result. The sample-size arithmetic exists so that you can tell "no difference" apart from "no data".

Bisecting a change history and slicing failures by segment exist for one reason: a drop in a headline number says nothing about its cause.

And the cost levers are ranked by risk. The cheapest saving is the one that cannot change an answer. The most expensive saving is the one that changes answers in the segment you can least afford.
158c80b5d6:
The professional exam describes a situation with numbers in it and offers four plausible designs. In this domain the right answer is nearly always the one that measures before it changes, changes one thing, protects the per-segment requirement and the latency SLA, and uses the simplest lever that works.

The wrong answers have shapes you can learn to spot:

  • switch to the biggest model;
  • rewrite the prompt without looking at failures;
  • stop the test as soon as the number looks good;
  • report an overall average that hides the failing segment;
  • save money with a lever nobody evaluated.

Other chapters own the instruments. Chapter 11 owns evaluation methodology (graders, golden sets, the three-state gate). Chapter 10 owns the telemetry this chapter reads. Chapter 5 owns the mechanics of context and caching. Here you meet them as tools, and the effort goes into the decisions.
1b5c9b70ed:
Almost none of this is new. A senior engineer who has run a staged production rollout already owns half of it.

What's new is the thing being changed. It is non-deterministic. It is judged by a metric that is itself noisy. It is priced per token. And it has to meet a threshold in every segment.

The statistics came from agriculture and medicine. The rollout machinery came from operations. Web products made the combination routine in the 2000s, and the LLM era added a cost line and a grading problem. It helps to know which piece answers which old failure.
c2211ca731:
Ronald Fisher's work on agricultural trials at Rothamsted in the 1920s, collected in The Design of Experiments (1935), made randomisation the foundation of causal claims. If the plots are assigned by chance, differences in yield can be put down to the treatment rather than the soil.

The 1948 Medical Research Council streptomycin trial is often cited as the first modern randomised clinical trial.

In the same decade Abraham Wald, working on munitions inspection, developed the sequential probability ratio test. Instead of fixing a sample size and looking once, you inspect as you go and stop when the evidence is strong enough. That is the ancestor of every modern "can I stop the A/B test early?" method. It came with a warning attached: you pay for the flexibility somewhere.
dc9a63c928:
Edward Simpson (1951) described the reversal that now carries his name. A treatment can win inside every subgroup and still lose in the pooled data, when the subgroups are unevenly represented in the two arms.

Quinn McNemar (1947) gave the test for paired binary outcomes. That's the one you need when the same case goes through both systems. Sture Holm (1979) gave a step-down correction for testing several hypotheses that is never less powerful than Bonferroni.

In medicine, stopping a trial early can save lives or waste a cure. Stuart Pocock (1977) and Peter O'Brien and Thomas Fleming (1979) published group-sequential boundaries for that setting. They allow a small, fixed number of interim looks while holding the overall false-positive rate at its nominal value. Example 05 in the companion folder reproduces both by simulation.
b0f5e44705:
Web companies found that when a change can ship to a random half of users in an afternoon, the experiment is cheaper than the argument.

Ron Kohavi and colleagues documented the practice, in their 2009 survey and the 2020 book Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. The lessons that matter here:

  • randomise by user;
  • check that the arms received the traffic you planned (the sample-ratio mismatch check, section 07);
  • watch guardrail metrics;
  • distrust results that are too good;
  • expect most ideas not to move the metric.

Operations contributed the canary release and the dark launch. You expose a new version to a few percent of traffic, or send it a copy of traffic whose responses are thrown away, before you commit.

Git added git bisect in its early years. It turned "something broke in the last six weeks" into a logarithmic search. Section 14 uses the same idea on a prompt-and-index history.
2820331127: Then teams started watching the experiment dashboard every morning, and that habit broke the assumptions of the classical test. Always-valid inference was designed to stay valid whenever you choose to stop. The mixture sequential probability ratio test described by Johari and colleagues is one example. Section 10 shows what these methods cost in sample size and in biased estimates, and where they still don't remove the need for a plan.
fe3d289fa4:
When the component under test is a language model, three things change.

First, outcomes are often judged by another model or by a human, so the metric has its own error (chapter 11). Second, the same input can produce different outputs on two runs, so a regression can be one unlucky sample. Third, every candidate has a price per token and a latency profile.

So "better" is a vector: quality per segment, p95 latency, cost per resolved case. The rest of the chapter works with that vector.
414c1ffee6:
A web team testing a button colour has a cheap, clean metric (clicks). It has no per-segment legal threshold. Its variant costs the same as the control.

An LLM team has none of these luxuries, and the differences shape every section that follows. They're worth listing once, plainly. Several exam distractors are just the web playbook applied without the adjustments.
9194baefe5:
The metric is usually graded, not observed. "Correct answer" is not a column in the database. It comes from a code check (exact match on a plan name), a model judge, a human reviewer, or a proxy that users generate: did they call back within seven days, did they escalate to an agent?

Each source has its own error and its own delay. Behavioural proxies are unbiased but slow and diluted. Judged scores are fast but need calibration against humans (chapter 11, section 13). A good online experiment names a behavioural primary metric where it can, and treats the judged score as a diagnostic.
2d89be6f02:
The requirement is per segment. Take a literal requirement such as "at least 95 percent in each of billing, roaming, device and plan change". A variant that raises the overall rate and drops roaming by four points fails it.

So the experiment needs a per-segment analysis plan and per-segment power. That's why section 06 computes days of traffic for the smallest segment, not the total. Overall averages are summaries for dashboards. Decisions are made on segments.
c89e6b0e1f:
Variants have a price. A shadow run duplicates inference cost. A larger model changes cost per request by a multiple. A longer prompt changes both cost and time to first token.

Cost and latency are therefore guardrails, and sometimes the primary metric. That makes "no quality difference" a good result for a cost-reduction experiment. It also needs a different statistical frame (non-inferiority, section 08) from "variant is better".
370f300a74:
The unit of randomisation and the unit of analysis differ. A customer has several conversations a week, and they are correlated: a customer with a prepaid plan asks prepaid questions.

Randomise by customer. Analyse by customer, or correct for clustering. Size the test with the clustering in mind (the design effect in section 06).

Randomising by request lets one customer see both arms inside one conversation, and the arms interfere. Example 06 measures 75 percent contamination in a three-request window.
44bc7dd8d0: Outputs are noisy, so some regressions are not real. If a case passes 80 percent of the time on the same input, a single failing run proves nothing. The experiment design absorbs this through sample size. The diagnosis workflow (section 16) absorbs it through repeated runs when a verdict decides a route.
3d7144ae08: The population moves. New products, a marketing campaign or a billing-cycle date all change what customers ask. A before-and-after comparison mistakes a change in the question mix for a change in the model. The remedy is a concurrent control arm for decisions, and mix-versus-rate decomposition for diagnosis (section 15).
d15938618a:
A Java/Spring reader can map most of this to what they already do:

  • feature flags with percentage rollout are the experiment assignment layer;
  • Micrometer tags are the arm label;
  • Spring Cloud Gateway or a servlet filter is the traffic mirror;
  • a scheduled job reading Prometheus counters is the canary controller.

The new part is the statistics on a graded, per-segment, priced metric. Sections 05 to 13 supply that.
fc98a672c0:
An LLM change can fail in ways the offline evaluation didn't cover. Real users ask things the golden set lacks. Latency under real concurrency differs from latency in a notebook. Costs move with real context sizes. And users change their behaviour when the answers change.

So a change climbs a ladder. Each rung exposes more risk, and only after the previous rung has produced evidence.

The ladder is not a ceremony for every edit. A typo fix in a prompt can go from offline evaluation straight to a canary. A model swap goes through all four rungs.
fbba5aaa3b:
Shadow mode is the most underused rung. For a Java architect it is a dark launch behind a traffic mirror.

Its special value for LLM changes is the paired output: the same live request answered by control and candidate. That is statistically much more efficient (section 09), and the disagreements are exactly the cases worth reading.

It has two hazards. One is cost: a mirror of 100 percent of traffic doubles inference spend (section 12). The other is side effects. A candidate that can issue a credit or send a message must run against stubs, and the guard that enforces this should fail loudly if anyone ever bypasses it.
16d76e38a3:
Canary and A/B test are not alternatives. They answer different questions.

A canary answers "is it safe to be on?". It is judged by guardrails against base plus margin, with automatic rollback. An A/B test answers "is it better?". It is judged by the primary metric at a planned sample size.

A common production pattern runs the canary first, at 1 to 5 percent, as the safety rung. Then it widens the same exposure to 50 percent as the experiment. The arms stay fixed, so nobody changes arm during the ramp (section 07).
12f9b43db0:
Which rungs a change needs follows from what it can break. A rule of thumb that works in review:

  • A change to wording inside the system prompt needs offline evaluation plus a canary.
  • A change to retrieval (chunking, index, reranker threshold) needs offline evaluation, shadow, and a canary. It changes which facts reach the model, on cases your golden set may not contain.
  • A model swap or a reasoning-budget change needs all four, because it changes cost, latency and behaviour together.
  • A new tool needs shadow in dry-run mode and a canary with the write path gated.

The test isn't whether the change is large. It's whether the golden set covers the failure the change could introduce.
acc6035471:
For the exam, notice what each rung cannot do.

Offline evaluation cannot show that real traffic looks like the golden set (chapter 11, section 18).

A canary at 1 percent cannot show that a guardrail is within margin. It can only show that nothing is grossly wrong. 300 conversations give an escalation-rate interval of about plus or minus 3.7 points (example 09, section 13).

An A/B test cannot rescue a change that was never safe to expose. So suppose a question offers "run a full A/B test on 50 percent of users straight away" for a prompt that has never seen real traffic. That's a distractor. The answer with a smaller first exposure and an automatic rollback is better, even if it is slower.
a9e99faa80:
A pre-registration is a short document, written before the first user is exposed. It states what will be measured, what counts as success, and what will be done with each outcome.

Its purpose is to take away the analyst's freedom after the fact. If the primary metric can be chosen after looking, then ten metrics and four segments give forty chances for a spurious win. A team that is motivated to ship will find one. Writing the decision rule first turns the experiment into a procedure.
22cb3eb74c:
The fields come from the requirements card (chapter 1, section 05):

  • The primary metric and its baseline come from the card's outcome and baseline.
  • The guardrails come from its constraints: per-segment accuracy, escalation rate, p95 latency, safety block rate, cost per outcome.
  • The minimum detectable effect comes from the ROI model (chapter 1, section 11). An effect smaller than the one that pays for the change isn't worth detecting.
  • The segments come from the card's segment list.
  • The kill switch and its owner come from the governance section of the card.

If a field can't be filled, the card is incomplete. That's a finding in itself.
3f2e8271c9:
Each rule is there because of a failure that shows up in real experiment programmes.

  • "Margin must be a number": a guardrail written as "no worse" cannot be tested. With enough data any difference is detectable, and with little data none is. So the rule needs a tolerance, such as one point of escalation or 0.4 seconds of p95.
  • "Unit must be user or account, not request": the contamination reason in section 03.
  • "Stopping must name a fixed n or a sequential method": see section 10.
  • "Duration must cover a weekly cycle": Monday and Saturday traffic differ in mix and in tone.
  • "Name the kill switch and its owner": a rollback with no owner takes hours at night.
  • "Single change": so that a win can be attributed and a loss can be debugged. If you must bundle, plan an ablation (section 14) for afterwards.
715f06f08c:
The second half of the output is the part to remember. The decision function takes the registration and a result and returns exactly one of SHIP, HOLD, ROLLBACK or INVALID. The four cases show why each exists:

  • A clean win ships.
  • A win with a breached latency guardrail rolls back. The guardrail was written down as a condition, not a hint.
  • A non-significant lift holds. It neither ships nor proves harm, and the registered options are to extend to the planned n or keep control.
  • A sample-ratio mismatch invalidates the whole result before anyone reads a metric.

Code that makes the decision from a registration, rather than a meeting that makes it from a dashboard, is the closest thing the discipline has to a unit test.
84a8d4994e: A scenario describes a team that "ran the test for a week, checked daily, and shipped when the resolution rate was significant". The answer names the missing pre-registration elements: a fixed n or sequential method, and guardrails with margins. It doesn't name a tool. A distractor suggests a more powerful statistical test. But the problem is the procedure, not the test.
3bd931b627:
A significance test answers one question. If there were no difference, how often would data this extreme occur? It says nothing about whether the experiment could see the difference you care about.

That second property is power: the probability that the test reports a difference when the true difference is the one you planned for. A test with 30 percent power misses a real improvement seven times in ten. A team that reads "not significant" as "no effect" throws away good changes.

So the sample size is computed before the experiment, from four inputs:

  • the baseline rate;
  • the minimum detectable effect, the smallest improvement worth shipping;
  • the significance level, usually 5 percent two-sided;
  • the power, usually 80 percent.
8c0d78fc2f:
The minimum detectable effect is the one input that's a business decision rather than a statistical one. It comes from the ROI model.

Say a three-point lift in first-contact resolution is worth the engineering and the extra token cost. Then three points is the effect to design for. A one-point lift that can't pay for itself isn't worth the days of traffic needed to detect it.

Detectable effect and sample size are tied by a square: halve the effect you want to detect and you need four times the users. Example 01 prints the table.
27bc971f61:
The formula assumes each observation is independent. Suppose the unit of randomisation is the customer, and a customer contributes several conversations whose outcomes are correlated. Then the effective sample is smaller.

The inflation is the design effect: 1 + (m - 1) times the intra-user correlation, where m is the number of conversations per user in the window. Three conversations per user at a correlation of 0.30 needs 1.6 times the users. Six conversations at 0.30 needs 2.5 times. Example 01 prints these.

The practical rule is to analyse at the level you randomise. Aggregate to one outcome per user, or use a cluster-robust method, and size the test to match.
42c185b521:
The literal requirement is per segment. So "how long?" is answered for the smallest segment you must decide on.

At 30,000 conversations a day split 50/50, the +3 point test is powered overall in 0.3 days. Roaming (15 percent of traffic) takes 1.6 days, and plan change (10 percent) takes 2.4 days. If the lift worth detecting is only +1 point, plan change needs 21.8 days.

Two things follow. First, run at least one full weekly cycle, and usually two, even if the arithmetic says two days. Monday and Saturday traffic differ.

Second, a rare segment sometimes can't be powered in a reasonable time. Say so in the registration, and choose among three honest options:

  • widen the interval you'll accept for that segment;
  • keep that segment on control;
  • pool it with a similar segment, on stated grounds.

What you must not do is report an overall win and let the rare segment ride along unmeasured.
605f37604b:
Randomisation is the one step that gives the comparison its meaning. It's also where most silent experiment failures start.

The implementation requirements are simple, and each has a failure mode behind it. The assignment must be:

  • deterministic: the same user gets the same arm on every call and every service instance, so no shared state is needed;
  • sticky across ramps: widening exposure must not move anyone to another arm;
  • independent across experiments: two concurrent experiments must not confound each other;
  • logged at assignment time: the analysis uses the arm the user was given, not an arm inferred later.
af52d260b0:
The standard implementation hashes a salt, the experiment name and the user ID to a bucket from 0 to 9999. Putting the experiment name inside the hash makes assignments independent across experiments.

The ramp rule is the part people get wrong. A first attempt puts the control in the lower half of the enrolled range. When exposure grows from 10 to 50 percent, the boundary moves and users change arms. Their outcomes then contain exposure to both treatments.

The fix is to set the control range once (buckets 0 to 4,999) and let the variant range grow from the top: 9,900 and up for 1 percent, 9,500 and up for 5 percent, and so on. Nobody ever changes arm. The unenrolled middle simply shrinks.
114c000e12:
If the plan is 50/50 and 50,000 users were assigned to each arm, the counts of users who reached analysis should be close to 50/50. If they aren't, something dropped users in a way that depends on the arm.

The common causes are mundane. The variant is slower and times out before its log line is written. A bot filter hits one arm. A redirect loses one arm's users. A cache serves the control from a path that skips logging.

The effect on the result isn't small, because the lost users are rarely random. The slow requests are the hard ones.

The check is a chi-square test of the arm counts against the plan, with a strict threshold (p below 0.001, so it rarely fires falsely). The second row of the output shows a variant that loses 2.2 percent of logs on timeout: 50,000 against 48,900, chi-square 12.2, p = 0.0005, INVALID.

The right reaction is to stop and debug before reading any metric. A significant lift on a population that lost its slowest cases in one arm is not evidence about the change.
882deeeb43:
The last line of the output is the argument for randomising by user. With per-request assignment and three requests in a window, 75 percent of users see both arms. Any outcome measured on the user then mixes the treatments: did they call back, did they churn, how did they rate the conversation?

For a conversation with several turns, the unit is at least the conversation. For a metric defined over a customer's week, it's the customer.
3752c33aa7:
The bucketer is a small component. It sits behind a servlet filter that runs after authentication. The filter resolves the arm once per request and puts it on the MDC and on the OpenTelemetry span (chapter 10). It also passes the arm to the prompt registry, so the arm selects the prompt version (chapter 5, section 18).

Both languages use the same hash. A Python batch job and a Spring service therefore assign the same user to the same arm, and the Java test in the companion folder checks that the numbers match.
cd999ca0f2:
When the planned sample has arrived, the analysis follows the registration and nothing else. There are three layers, and a decision uses all of them.

The primary metric is tested once, with the registered test, and reported with its confidence interval as well as its p-value. A lift of +1.49 points with an interval of [+0.01, +2.97] says the effect is probably real. It also says it could be anywhere from worthless to twice the point estimate.

The guardrails are tested for non-inferiority. The question isn't whether the variant is different. It's whether the worst plausible harm stays inside the written margin.

The segments are examined one at a time, because the requirement is per segment. A multiplicity correction makes sure that looking at four segments doesn't give you four chances to be fooled.
0abd8c20f4:
Read the output the way a reviewer would.

The overall primary result passes the registered threshold (p = 0.0491), but only just, and the lower end of the interval is +0.01 points. The registered minimum detectable effect was three points. So the experiment found an effect that is probably well below what the ROI model needed. Statistical significance is not the same as being worth shipping.

The overall escalation guardrail has a point difference of only +0.16 points. Its upper bound, though, is +1.27 points, over the 1.0 point margin, so non-inferiority is not demonstrated. That's the difference between "no evidence of harm" and "evidence of no important harm". The point estimate is not the test. The bound is.
e7e05eb918:
The segment table shows why the overall numbers mislead. Billing wins (+2.7 points, adjusted p = 0.044). Roaming loses 3.6 points of resolution, and its escalation rate is up 3.3 points with an upper bound of +6.7.

The variant didn't make the model worse everywhere. It made roaming worse, and billing, half the traffic, pulled the average up. A decision on the overall number ships a change that fails the roaming requirement.

The correct output is the one the example prints: HOLD for all. One option is a new, smaller, pre-registered experiment that ships the change only to the segments that win.
3d4101a7ba:
Test four segments at the 5 percent level and you have roughly a 19 percent chance of at least one false positive when nothing is happening.

The Holm step-down procedure orders the p-values from smallest to largest. It multiplies the smallest by 4, the next by 3, and so on, enforcing monotonicity. It controls the family-wise error rate and is never less powerful than the Bonferroni correction. In the example, billing's raw p of 0.0111 becomes 0.0444 and survives. Device and roaming (0.0563 and 0.0810) become 0.1689 and don't.

Sometimes the segments are the decision units for harm: a regression in any segment blocks shipping. Then correct the other way, and don't adjust the harm test. Missing a real regression costs more than a false alarm. The registration states which direction each test is conservative in.
64fa59fa14:
Online A/B tests compare two different groups of users. Offline evaluation and shadow mode compare two systems on the same cases. Ignoring that wastes information.

A hard case is hard for both systems. The unpaired test treats the two sets of results as unrelated samples, so it has to explain the case-to-case variation as noise. The paired test looks only at the cases where the systems disagree, and asks whether the disagreements lean one way.

For binary pass or fail outcomes the paired test is McNemar's. Count the cases only the control passed (b) and only the variant passed (c). Ignore the rest. Then test whether b and c differ from an even split.
478ea74ad1:
On 500 shared cases the control passes 441 and the variant 459. The unpaired two-proportion test gives p = 0.058 and says "not significant". The paired test sees only the 17 cases the control alone passed and the 35 only the variant passed. It gives an exact p of 0.018. Same data; the paired analysis just uses the structure.

The second table is the lesson to remember. As the two systems fail on more of the same cases (higher shared difficulty), the paired test's power grows from 27 to 54 percent. The unpaired test's power doesn't improve.

In practice, a shadow comparison on 500 mirrored requests can be a stronger test than an online A/B with several thousand users. That's one reason to use shadow mode before an A/B test. Chapter 11, section 15, makes the same point for offline comparisons and adds a paired bootstrap for continuous scores.
6f44d12a1f:
The exact McNemar test is a binomial tail on n = b + c discordant pairs. It takes eight lines in java/TwoProportionTest.java, and the companion run checks that it agrees with the Python function to the digit.

In an evaluation gate (chapter 11, section 19) it belongs next to the Wilson interval. Wilson says whether a segment clears the bar. McNemar says whether this build is better than that build on the same cases.
c010542e9b:
A fixed-sample test is valid under one condition: you look once, at the planned n.

Now put the p-value on a dashboard every morning, and let a product owner stop the test when it first falls under 0.05. The nominal 5 percent false-positive rate no longer holds. Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line.

Example 04 simulates A/A tests, where there is no difference at all, with 500 users per arm per day for 14 days.
733ba8ac79:
Look daily and stop at the first p below 0.05, and you get a false "win" in 21.9 percent of A/A tests. That's more than four times the advertised rate. The median day of the false win is day 4, exactly when the early, noisy, exciting numbers come in.

Seven looks give 16.8 percent. Two looks give 8.8 percent. The inflation grows slowly with the number of looks (roughly like the maximum of a random walk), but it never stops growing.
418d7166d2:
There are three honest responses.

The first is discipline. Pre-register one analysis at the planned n and don't report the primary metric earlier. The dashboard can show guardrails continuously, because guardrails stop a test for harm, and a false stop costs little.

The second is a group-sequential design. Plan a small number of looks and spend the 5 percent across them.

  • Pocock-type boundaries use the same critical value at every look (2.44 for five looks in example 05). Early stopping is easy, but the final look is strict.
  • O'Brien-Fleming-type boundaries are very strict early (4.54 at 20 percent of the data) and close to the usual value at the end (2.03). They protect against an early fluke and lose almost no power if the test runs to the end.

The constants in the example are calibrated by simulation so you can see where they come from. For production, use a validated library or the published tables.

The third is an always-valid method such as the mixture SPRT. Its evidence statistic is valid at any stopping time, so it suits a dashboard that people watch.
1ad650bb23: The estimate is biased when you stop early. The true lift is +3.00, yet among stopped trials the mean estimated lift is +4.46 points (Pocock-type) and +3.80 (O'Brien-Fleming-type). Trials that stop early are the ones where noise helped, so the winner's estimate is inflated. If the ROI model uses the estimate, shrink it or confirm it with a holdout.
ed5fbb510d: Sequential designs cost sample size or power somewhere. The Pocock-type design above has 69.8 percent power at the planned n, against 78.2 percent for the fixed test. In exchange it needs a smaller expected sample when there is an effect (2,529 per arm against 3,554). The mSPRT needs 4,179 per arm on average when there is an effect, and its false-positive rate is 1.8 percent: valid, but conservative.
5254a06975: The confidence interval must match the method. After a group-sequential or always-valid test, the usual plus or minus 1.96 standard errors is wrong. Use the interval the method defines (an always-valid or repeated-confidence interval). Or report only the decision and a conservative bound.
08af725ad6: Guardrail looks are different. A false rollback costs a few days. A missed regression costs customers. So guardrails are checked continuously, and a breach stops the test at once; the canary controller in section 13 does exactly this. Don't treat the primary metric and the guardrails with one rule.
9ffdfecd0a: A sequential test still needs a plan. It needs a maximum sample, the number and timing of looks (or the mixture prior for the mSPRT), and the same segment logic. "We will use a sequential test", with no maximum n and no per-segment plan, is not a registration.
02495cff57: "A product manager wants to stop the test on day 3 because the dashboard shows p = 0.03." The right answer says that repeated looks inflate the false-positive rate, to more than 20 percent for daily looks over two weeks. It then offers two compliant options: continue to the registered n, or pre-register a sequential design with an alpha-spending boundary and a maximum sample. The distractors are "lower the p threshold to 0.01" (with no stated justification) and "use a bigger model".
e4ff9d4963:
A latency SLA is stated on a percentile: p95 of time to complete at most 10 seconds, p95 time to first token at most 3 seconds. Testing a percentile is harder than testing a rate, for two reasons.

First, there's no simple closed-form variance for a percentile difference. The standard tool is the bootstrap. Resample each arm with replacement, compute the percentile difference, repeat 1,500 times, and read the interval off the sorted differences.

Second, a tail estimate depends on a few observations. Its interval is wide unless the sample is large.
2f30d14a6c:
The first block is the decision example. The variant's mean is 0.27 seconds slower, and its p95 is 0.38 seconds slower, inside a registered margin of 0.40 seconds. A rule on the point estimate says pass.

But the bootstrap interval is [+0.08, +0.75], and its upper bound is above the margin. So a rule on the bound says fail: not shown to be within margin. With control at a p95 of 9.5 seconds against a 10-second SLA, the true variant p95 could be as high as 10.25 seconds.

The decision rule that protects the SLA sits on the upper bound. The remedy for a wide interval is more data, not a looser rule.
c858aed147:
The second block is the sizing table. The p95 interval of a single arm is 1.76 seconds wide at 300 requests, 0.59 at 1,000 and 0.23 at 10,000. The p99 needs about ten times the data of the p95 for the same width (2.10 seconds wide at 300, 0.55 at 10,000).

So the percentile an SLA names is also a data-collection decision. A contract that says p99 needs a much larger canary to check than one that says p95.

The third block shows the per-segment tail. Overall p95 is 9.23 seconds, inside the SLA. Roaming's p95 is 11.96 seconds, outside it. An overall latency average hides a segment-level breach just as an overall accuracy does. Roaming here is the long-context, multi-tool route.
1716e9544b:
Cost per outcome is the third guardrail, and it needs the least statistics. It's a mean of a positive quantity, so a bootstrap or a normal interval on per-conversation cost is enough. You can compute it from the metering that chapter 10 (Part 6) sets up, tagged by experiment arm.

The denominator is what deserves care. A variant that cuts tokens by 30 percent and lowers resolution by 2 points may cost more per resolved conversation. Each failed resolution lands on a human, at several dollars of agent time. Section 22 builds that model and shows why the denominator is the outcome.
581d21b2a6:
Shadow mode answers the question offline evaluation can't. How does the candidate behave on the requests my customers actually send, including the ones my golden set doesn't contain?

The mechanism is a traffic mirror. The live path answers the user with the control, as before. A copy of the request goes asynchronously to the candidate. Its response is stored next to the control's, and nothing reaches the user. A grader, a diff report and a human reading the disagreements produce the evidence.
426574f5ba:
Look at what the mirror found. Agreement on the action taken is 83.7 percent, and the disagreements aren't random. In 64 cases the candidate acts (issues a credit) where the control only answers in text. In 34 it's the reverse. Overall, the control path issued 51 credits and the candidate would have issued 81.

A paired quality score could rate both answers equally well, while the candidate's credit behaviour is a cost and a policy risk. That's the value of looking at actions and not only at text. Tool calls are the side-effect surface.

The next step is human review of these disagreements, grouped by kind, before any canary.
00638429dd:
The guard is the part architects forget. The example wires the real credit function into the shadow path on purpose and shows that the guard raises.

In a production system the equivalent is a dependency-injected tool registry with two implementations, live and dry-run, selected by the request's mode. Add a unit test that the shadow mode registry contains no live implementation for any tool marked as a writer.

Remember that a prompt injection (chapter 13) in a shadowed request is as dangerous in shadow as in production if the tools are live.
2a37515a4f:
The cost line is the last table. At illustrative mid-tier prices and the cost profile of configuration B, mirroring 5 percent of traffic adds $1,333 a month. 25 percent adds $6,666, and 100 percent adds $26,662.

The sampling rule follows from the paired test. Mirror enough to reach the number of cases the registered power needs: a few hundred to a few thousand per segment that must be decided. Stratify so the rare segments are included. Then stop. Shadow is a pre-launch rung, not a permanent second system.

Its privacy treatment is the same as production's. The mirrored requests contain the same personal data, so they follow the same redaction, retention and access rules (chapter 10, Part 3; chapter 14).
82de94d295:
With Spring Cloud Gateway, a filter on the route can clone the request and send it to the candidate service with WebClient on a bounded-elastic scheduler, ignoring the response (fire and forget). Keep the mirror off the request thread and behind a circuit breaker, so a slow candidate can't slow the live path.

The tool registry is an ordinary Spring bean with a @Profile("shadow") or a request-scoped implementation. The guard is a test that scans beans of type WriterTool in the shadow context. Check your gateway version for exact mirror support, as the filter names vary.
75876f7a85:
A canary exposes a small share of real users to the candidate and watches guardrails. The design questions are what the controller compares, how many users each stage needs to prove anything, and what happens on a breach.

The last question has the simplest answer. The rollback is automatic. It's a feature flag flip, and a named owner gets paged. A rollback decision that waits for a meeting is a rollback measured in hours.
fb822e7f50:
The comparison is a one-sided interval check on each guardrail. For a rate such as escalation, compute the Wilson interval of the canary's own observed rate. Then:

  • If the whole interval is above base plus margin, roll back. The harm is established.
  • If the whole interval is below base plus margin, the guardrail is shown within margin and the stage may advance.
  • Otherwise, wait for more data.

This is the same three-state logic as the evaluation gate of chapter 11 (section 06), applied to a stream. Latency uses the p95 of the canary against the SLA, plus the bootstrap of section 11 when the margin is tight.
f0c7a7daf7:
Four candidates went through the same controller.

The healthy one advanced through 1, 5 and 25 percent and reached full rollout in 6 further hours, with monitoring kept on.

The subtle candidate had a true escalation rate three points above the base. It passed the 1 percent smoke stage, because an interval of plus or minus 3.7 points can't see a three point drift. It was rolled back in the 5 percent stage after 30 hours and 1,875 conversations.

The slow tail candidate was rolled back at 1 percent, because its p95 of 11.7 seconds exceeded the 10-second SLA. Gross latency failures show up in a small sample. The tail is the whole point.

The error spike was rolled back after 18 hours, at 4.0 percent errors against a 0.5 percent base.
5ca5d3fdaa:
Three design rules come out of the table.

Size the stage by the margin. If the margin is 2 points on a 12 percent base, the smallest stage that can prove "within margin" needs about 1,500 conversations (a half-width of 1.6 points). Label the 1 percent stage for what it is: a smoke detector, with a threshold of three times the margin in the example.

Time is part of the stage. Each stage has a minimum duration, 24 hours here, even if the count is met sooner, so that it sees a night and a morning. The final decision to advance still requires the interval, not just the clock.

The controller needs a stuck state. Traffic may be lower than assumed, and a stage may fail to prove within margin after 96 hours. The controller then reports it instead of looping. The remedy is to extend, widen the margin with a stated reason, or redesign the experiment.
adc6187030:
Quality regressions rarely announce themselves with an exception. The resolution rate slips two points over three weeks. Or the judged pass rate on roaming falls from 97 to 93 percent. Or the escalation rate creeps up on Thursdays.

The first instinct is to open the prompt and edit it. That instinct is usually wrong, and the reason is arithmetic. The system has many components: prompt, model snapshot, retrieval index, chunking, reranker, tool schemas, client libraries, the world's questions. An edit to one leaves the others untouched and the cause unfound.

The discipline is to ask a fixed sequence of questions, ordered by how cheaply each one discriminates.
4db7b2a53a:
The order matters for cost. Questions 1 to 3 cost minutes and a query against the telemetry of chapter 10. They decide whether there's a model problem at all. Question 4 costs a handful of builds when bisected. Question 5 costs model calls, about 1.4 per failing case in example 12.

Only after these does anyone design a fix. Even then it's a hypothesis with a predicted effect on a named segment, tested like any other change in this chapter.
6b70d905d0:
Say the build was good on 2 June and bad on 18 August, and twelve things changed in between. A linear search tests up to twelve builds. Bisection tests about four.

The classic assumption is that behaviour is monotone: once the culprit is in, every later build is bad. Two LLM-specific complications need handling.

The evaluation is noisy, so a verdict has to be statistical. Compare each candidate build with the known-good build on every segment, with a one-sided test. Call a build bad only when the evidence is clear. Call it good when the evidence is clear. Collect more cases when the answer is grey.

And the history may contain more than one defect, or a defect that needs two changes. Bisection doesn't find those by itself.
bc3670b4f7:
Read the output again for two lessons.

First, the cost: 217,600 graded cases in the session. Grey verdicts double the sample (400 to 800 to 1,600 to 3,200 cases per segment), and each revert is evaluated at 3,200. That argues for caching graded results per (build, case), and for small, stratified regression sets that run fast in CI (chapter 11, section 17).

Second, the method. Bisect searches for the first bad change. A good diagnosis always ends with the ablation that tests the claim "this change is necessary" by reverting it from head. A fix that hasn't been confirmed by revert-and-measure is a story.
190a78f49a:
"Resolution fell from 72 to 69 percent over three weeks. The team proposes rewriting the system prompt and moving to a larger model." The professional answer runs the order of questions. Confirm the drop with an interval and check the grader. Decompose by segment and input mix. List what changed and bisect. Triage a sample of failures by component.

It edits nothing before it knows where the failures are. The distractors are the two proposals in the stem. Each is a hypothesis without a test.
c57c0adf80:
Trace analysis turns the telemetry of chapter 10 into hypotheses. A trace carries the request, the segment, the retrieved document IDs, the tool calls, the token counts, the arm and the grader's verdict. Where the pipeline is instrumented that way, it also carries a failure category.

The analysis has two tools. A decomposition separates changes in what customers ask from changes in how well we answer. A ranking finds the slices where failures concentrate.
16b741e1ee:
Suppose the overall failure rate rose from 2.96 percent in week 1 to 4.44 percent in week 5. Two different things can raise an average. The failure rate inside each segment can rise: the system got worse. Or the traffic can move toward segments that were always worse: the system is the same and the questions changed.

The decomposition is exact. For each segment, take weights w (share of traffic) and r (failure rate) in weeks 0 and 1.

  • The mix term is (w1 - w0) x r0: the movement of traffic, valued at the old rate.
  • The rate term is w1 x (r1 - r0): the change in rate, weighted at the new traffic.

The terms sum to the total change.
48f92bc40c:
The overall change is +1.47 points. Only +0.08 of it is the mix term; the rate term is +1.39. That points inside the segments, and almost all of it is roaming. Its traffic share rose from 15 to 26 percent, and its failure rate from 3.5 to 8.2 percent.

If the rate terms had been near zero and the mix term large, the conclusion would be different. Nothing got worse; the question mix moved. The response would then be to extend the golden set and the launch plan for the segment that grew, not to change the model.
c18aea98a9:
Within roaming, which requests fail? Start by defining candidate slices from the trace features: segment, channel, language, whether the request mentions a product name unknown to the catalogue, customer tier, input length bucket. For each slice, compute its failure rate now and before. Then rank slices by the change in their share of all failures.

Two-dimensional slices catch interactions that one-dimensional slices hide. Enforce a minimum count per slice (300 requests in the example), so tiny slices don't dominate the ranking.
cb73bc0316:
The top slice is unknown product names inside roaming. It holds 3 percent of failures in week 1 and 36 percent in week 5.

Now look at its own failure rate: 32.5 percent in week 1 and 31.3 percent in week 5. It didn't change. What changed is how much traffic falls into it, because a launch introduced new product names (the example simulates this).

The model didn't degrade. The world moved into a region the evaluation set covers poorly, which is the dataset-drift case of chapter 11, section 18. The remedy is content and data. Put the new products in the catalogue and the index. Add cases to the golden set. Add a metric on the share of requests with unknown entities.

Treat the ranking as a list of hypotheses to test, not conclusions. Slices overlap, and shares don't sum to 100 percent.
24daf6dead:
The last block is the experiment version of the same arithmetic. The variant has a lower failure rate in both billing (2.7 against 3.0 percent) and roaming (9.0 against 10.0 percent). Yet its overall failure rate is higher (7.7 against 3.8 percent). A ramp bug sent the variant mostly roaming traffic, which fails more often.

Pooled comparison of unbalanced arms is wrong. Two controls prevent it. Check the sample-ratio mismatch per segment, not just overall. And report the segment-level comparison first; if someone wants an overall number, combine segments with fixed weights (the population shares).
06a081eb6d:
Once the failures are located, the next question is which component owns each failing case. The fix differs completely. A prompt edit, an index change, a model change, a content addition and a label correction each have different costs and different risks.

The method is triage by controlled substitution. Take a sample of failing cases and change one thing at a time while holding the others fixed. Use only what a team can observe: retrieved IDs, gold IDs, model outputs.
5b8964c84b:
Walk the procedure.

No gold document exists in the corpus for the case. That's a content gap, and no model change can fix it. The right behaviour is to say it doesn't know and route the question to content owners.

The gold chunk was not retrieved. Re-run with the gold chunk handed to the model. If it now passes on the same prompt and model, the fault is retrieval. If it passes only with a clearer prompt, it is retrieval plus prompt.

The right chunk was retrieved and the answer is still wrong. Try a larger model with the same prompt. If that fixes it, it's a model mismatch: the tier is too small for this case type. If not, try a clearer instruction on the same model. If that fixes it, it's a prompt fault. If only both together fix it, it's prompt plus model.

If nothing fixes it, the case goes to a reading queue. The gold label may be wrong, or the case may be unsolved with this design.
872f9932e2:
Hallucination fits this scheme as a symptom with several possible causes. A claim that appears in the answer but not in the retrieved context is ungrounded.

If the gold chunk was missing, the model filled the gap, so the fault is retrieval (or a content gap). If the chunk was present and the model still invented a detail, the fault is the prompt or the model tier. Maybe the prompt didn't forbid answering from memory, or didn't give the model a defined way to say it doesn't know.

A grounding check turns this from an impression into a measured rate per segment. Every factual claim in the answer must be supported by a quoted span from the context (chapter 13).
0d85c336cb:
Read the result honestly, with two warnings.

The perfect agreement (100 percent) in the confusion matrix is true by construction. The example plants a hidden root cause per case and shows that the procedure recovers it. Real systems have interactions the four-way scheme doesn't name, and a judge that is itself sometimes wrong.

And the scheme is only as good as its re-runs. A model can disagree with itself, so one run per condition is unreliable. The second half of the output simulates 8 percent random verdict flips. Single-run agreement is 90 percent, majority of three is 98 percent and majority of five is 100 percent, at 140, 435 and 710 model calls.

Use single runs to discover the large classes. Repeat only when the verdict will decide a route or a model tier.
b6e0e51adc: "Accuracy on roaming dropped. Failures show the right answer was in the corpus. Which action first?" The answer: check whether the right chunk was retrieved before touching the prompt or model. If retrieval missed it, no prompt can fix it. If retrieval found it, a controlled substitution (larger model, clearer prompt) says which of the other two owns the fault. "Increase the context size" and "switch to the largest model" are the distractors.
159d5d16c2:
Cost work on an LLM system has the same shape as performance work on a service. Measure where the money goes. Rank the levers by saving per unit of risk. Change one thing at a time. Keep a change only if the things that must not move didn't move.

The unit of cost is the one from chapter 1: the cost of a business outcome, such as a resolved conversation or a processed order. It's built from the cost of model calls plus the cost of the humans and retries those calls cause. For a model call, the cost is arithmetic on token counts.
2feff46e01:
Four things move the first line:

  • the number of tokens in: prompt, retrieved context, history, tool results;
  • the number of tokens out, which cost several times more per token and dominate latency;
  • the model tier, which sets the price per token;
  • the share of input tokens read from cache, at a fraction of the price.

The first four levers below map to those terms. The fifth, batch, changes the price for work nobody is waiting on. The sixth, the number of calls per outcome, is a design lever (chapter 2): fewer round trips, no redundant verification calls, no agent loop where a workflow will do.
00b79061da:
Apply the levers in order of risk, not size.

A saving that can't change an output, such as caching a byte-identical prefix, goes first. It needs no quality gate beyond a regression check. Measured trims come second, each gated. A change of model or of reasoning budget comes last, because it changes answers on exactly the hardest and rarest cases.

Example 13 applies the levers in that order to a baseline of the care assistant, with illustrative prices and token counts. It gates every step on all four segments, with a Wilson lower bound against 0.95 on 4,000 cases per segment. It also requires that p95 doesn't get worse.
27f4748dad:
Three observations, stated plainly.

First, the cheapest configuration in the table is not the answer. Haiku for all segments is 89 percent cheaper than the baseline, and it fails the roaming requirement (lower bound 0.923 against the 0.95 gate). So it's rejected. The exam wants exactly that behaviour: the per-segment requirement is literal.

Second, the same smaller model passes on billing (lower bound 0.960). So the route keeps the saving where the evidence supports it.

Third, the parallel-tools step doesn't change cost at all. It's in the table because latency is a constraint the levers must respect (section 21). It's the step that brings p95 from 11.1 seconds to 9.7.
4d07b8199d:
Chapter 5 (sections 12 to 15) explains how prompt caching works. A first request pays a write premium to store a prefix of the request. Later requests that share the byte-identical prefix within the time-to-live pay a fraction of the normal input price to read it. Each read refreshes the entry.

This section is about the decision, because caching is a bet on traffic. Use the placeholder multipliers of the example (read 0.10, five-minute write 1.25, one-hour write 2.0). Check the docs for the current ones, for the minimum cacheable length, and for which time-to-live options exist.
9514e03686:
The break-even is one line of algebra. Let h be the share of requests that find a live entry. The relative cost of the cached prefix is h x 0.10 + (1 - h) x write. Caching wins when that is below 1, so h must exceed (write - 1) / (write - 0.10). That's 21.7 percent for a 1.25 write and 52.6 percent for a 2.0 write.

Hit rate depends on the request rate for each distinct prefix. With arrivals roughly Poisson at rate lambda per minute and a time-to-live of T minutes, the chance that the previous request for the same prefix arrived inside the window is 1 - exp(-lambda x T).
d24ffb06be:
The routes table shows the two ways caching goes wrong.

The first is a low-traffic route: a new market with 0.02 requests a minute per prefix. It has a hit rate of 10 percent with a 5-minute entry. It pays the write premium on nine requests in ten and costs $0.0290 per request, against $0.0267 uncached. Caching made it more expensive. The 1-hour entry costs $0.0213 and wins for that route, because the longer window raises the hit rate enough to pay for the higher write price.

The second failure is a prefix that isn't shared. The "name in prefix" row puts the customer's name in the cached portion. The one shared prefix becomes 120,000 private prefixes, each seen once. The hit rate is 0, and the route pays the write premium on every request ($0.0308 against $0.0267, and $0.0428 on the 1-hour entry). A longer time-to-live won't fix this. Move per-request tokens after the cache breakpoint and keep the prefix byte-identical (chapter 5, section 14).

On busy routes the saving is large. It comes to about $33,000 a month across the four main routes at these illustrative prices and volume, for a change that doesn't alter any output.
98b4614dbf:
Verify; don't assume. Chapter 10 describes the usage fields on the response that report tokens read from and written to the cache (check the docs for exact field names). The monitoring check is a daily hit rate per route against the break-even above.

A rollout that renames a section of the system prompt, or adds a timestamp to the top of it, silently drops the hit rate to zero on every route. The first symptom is the invoice. That's a regression with a diagnosis (section 14, question 4) and an alert (chapter 10, Part 5).
f43c472e30:
Model tiers differ in price per token, speed and capability. The decision is made per segment, on evidence, because the requirement is per segment. Chapter 4 explains model selection, and chapter 1, section 15 introduces routing as an economic decision.

The structure that works: start every segment at a tier known to be safe. Move a segment down only when the evaluation at that tier proves it clears the gate.

"Proves" has a number behind it. With 100 cases per segment, nothing can be proved below the top tier. Even a 97 percent segment has a Wilson lower bound too low to clear 95 percent (chapter 11, section 07).
f632cba7e4:
The first table is a lesson about evidence. With 100 cases per segment, every segment stays on the largest tier, at $44,438 a month. With 300 cases only roaming can move to the mid tier. At 1,000 cases billing can go to the small tier and the rest to the mid tier ($17,775). At 4,000 cases device also moves to the small tier ($13,331).

The routing uses the same set of models throughout. What changed is the amount of evidence. That's why the cheap tier isn't "free": you buy the saving with evaluation cases. For a rare segment, the cases cost more than the saving.
c95bc73956:
The second table is about the router. A cascade or a classifier that sends requests to different tiers has its own error rate. The dangerous direction is a hard request sent to the small tier.

The tolerance depends on the gap between the tiers on that segment. Say the small tier is at 0.931 on roaming and the mid tier at 0.971. The router can then misroute 38 percent of roaming requests to the small tier and still keep the expected rate above the gate plus an interval allowance. If the small tier were at 0.88 on roaming, the tolerance would fall to 16 percent.

So the router is a component with a confusion matrix evaluated per segment, and that confusion matrix goes into the gate.

The router call itself is cheap but not free: 400 input tokens and 20 output on the small tier, $0.0005 per request, 4.2 percent of one mid-tier answer. A cascade that escalates 60 percent of traffic costs more than not cascading at all.
4a341ef390:
The Message Batches API processes requests asynchronously at a discount (50 percent in the examples; check the docs for current terms). Results come back within a time window of up to a day (check the docs).

It's the right lever for work with no user waiting:

  • nightly classification of the day's tickets;
  • re-scoring a golden set;
  • summarising call transcripts;
  • backfilling embeddings' companion metadata;
  • the offline half of the experiments in this chapter, such as grading a shadow sample or running regression sets.

It's the wrong lever for interactive turns. It also doesn't support multi-turn tool conversations in the middle of a batch, because nobody is there to answer the tool call (check the docs for what tool use is supported).

The decision is a latency requirement, not a cost preference. If the SLA is "within 24 hours", batch is half the price. If it's "within 10 seconds", batch is unavailable.

Batch combines with caching, so a batch of requests sharing a long prefix pays both reductions. Check the docs for how cache hits behave inside batches, because ordering and timing are not guaranteed.
3c3a0eaa6c: "A nightly job classifies 800,000 tickets with a 6-hour window. The team proposes moving to a smaller model to cut cost." The better answer first asks whether the work is interactive. It isn't, so it moves to batch for the discount with no quality change. Evaluating the smaller model per segment is a separate, later step. A distractor that changes the model first takes the risk before taking the free saving.
c5bab6f1fc:
Two levers are cheaper than any model change, and both follow from the asymmetry in the cost formula.

Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens at the illustrative prices: five times for the mid tier, $15 against $3. They're also generated one at a time, so output length dominates completion time. In the care assistant, 650 output tokens at 80 tokens a second is about 8.1 seconds of a 10.5-second median call. Prefill of 9,100 tokens takes about a second.

So shortening the answer is the strongest single latency lever, and a strong cost lever too. Trimming the context is the strongest lever on input cost. The cheapest token is the one that never enters the window (chapter 5, section 08).
338446bba9: Retrieve fewer, better chunks. In example 13, reranking twelve candidates to four removed 2,100 fresh input tokens per request. It moved the worst-segment lower bound by only 0.004 (0.959 to 0.955). The gate decides whether that trade is acceptable. Watch the segment where the removed chunks mattered, usually the one with multi-document answers (chapter 9).
411fa01e5b: Constrain the format. A structured answer, such as a JSON object with a short answer field and a citation field, is shorter than prose and parseable. Example 13 cut output from 650 to 380 tokens, and the worst segment moved from 0.955 to 0.962 because the shorter format also removed rambling. Don't assume that will happen. Measure it, since cutting reasoning text can also cut correct reasoning.
ab3d69524e: Set the cap deliberately. max_tokens is a safety limit, not a style control. A cap below the natural length truncates the answer and produces stop_reason: max_tokens, so alert on its rate (chapter 10). Set the cap at the p99 of the length distribution of good answers, plus a margin. If the p99 is far above what a good answer needs, fix the prompt.
614919cd6e: Drop what is stale. Tool results older than the current step, repeated system boilerplate, and a long history re-sent every turn grow the bill quadratically over a session (chapter 5, section 06). Clear or summarise at the source. Then cache what stays stable.
d37c3fc740: Reasoning budget. Extended or adaptive thinking trades tokens and latency for accuracy on hard cases (check the docs for the parameter and its model support). Treat the budget as a lever of the highest risk class. In example 13, lowering it saved money and failed the roaming gate (0.934). The extra reasoning was exactly what hard roaming cases needed.
1386ad1ad7: Length is also a measurement problem. Log input and output tokens per request, segment and arm (chapter 10, Part 6). Look at the distribution, not only the mean. And keep a length regression among the guardrails of any prompt experiment. A "better" prompt that triples output length has a cost and a latency the quality metric won't show.
38c3354711:
Latency gets the same discipline: decompose before changing. A request's time to complete has three parts:

  • the data and tool calls before the model;
  • the time to first token: queueing plus prefill of the input, which scales with fresh input tokens and is much faster for cached ones;
  • generation: output tokens divided by decode speed.

Each lever removes a different term, and the SLA names a specific term. It might be p95 of time to complete at 10 seconds, or p95 of first token at 3 seconds with streaming on.

A lever that helps the wrong term is a waste. A stream that makes the first token fast does nothing for a client that needs the whole JSON object before it can proceed.
d08433bc03:
Read the order of the table, because it runs against intuition.

Parallelising the three independent data calls saves 0.8 seconds at the p95, and caching saves 0.5. Neither gets near the SLA. Cutting the output from 650 to 380 tokens saves 5.5 seconds, because decode time dominates.

Streaming then leaves completion unchanged and moves the perceived start from 9.7 to 2.3 seconds. It's the right lever only when the SLA is on the first token, or when the human reads while the model writes.

Hedging means starting a second request when the first hasn't produced a token in 2 seconds, and taking whichever answers first. It trims the p99 from 19.1 to 17.6 seconds. The price is extra requests on the slowest few percent, and the cost model must count them.

The smaller model on an easy route reaches a 6.2 second p95 and a 10.7 second p99.
c5b1dd0191:
Three cautions.

Add levers one at a time and re-measure. Latencies don't add: the p95 of a sum is not the sum of p95s. That's why the example simulates them rather than adding.

Parallelism needs independence. Tool calls that depend on each other's results can't run together. The model can emit several independent tool calls in one turn, and your code should execute those concurrently (check the docs on parallel tool use).

A latency lever can break the quality gate. A smaller model, fewer chunks and a shorter reasoning budget all appear here. Each has to pass section 17's gate before it counts.

Chapter 1, section 13 treats latency as the constraint that disqualifies designs. This section treats it as the constraint the optimisations must still meet.
91719fe1d5:
The cost of tokens is usually the smaller part of the cost of an automated process. When a conversation fails to resolve and lands on an agent, the agent's eight minutes at a loaded $0.85 a minute cost $6.80. That's hundreds of times the token cost of the conversation. A design that saves a tenth of a cent per request and loses two points of resolution is a loss.

So the model that compares designs uses the cost per outcome. Take all costs of a conversation (tokens, grading, retrieval infrastructure, the human cost of escalations, fixed upkeep) and divide by the conversations that resolved without a human.
927840e39e:
Read it in three passes.

Design C loses. Haiku everywhere has the cheapest tokens ($0.0117 a conversation), the most expensive outcome ($1.800 a resolved conversation) and a negative monthly margin. Resolution drops to 66 percent, and 17 percent of conversations reach an agent.

Design A against B shows the direct value of the cost levers. Caching and trimming take $1.302 to $1.214 with no change in resolution.

Design D, billing on the smaller model, is level with B ($1.214), not better. That's useful information. The gate allowed it, but the unit economics say it isn't worth the router's complexity at these numbers. Add a routing component only when it pays for itself. The simplest architecture that works wins.
9df0ff8e3c:
Design E, the largest model, wins on paper. It costs more per token and resolves 1.2 points more. At these numbers that takes cost per resolved conversation to $1.108, and monthly margin from $248,647 to $321,592. The output states the break-even: the larger model only needs to lift resolution by 0.25 points over B to match B's cost per resolved conversation.

But the table assumes a lift of 1.2 points, and that isn't a design input. It's the thing an A/B test measures. Section 06 says a 1-point lift on a 70 percent base needs 32,647 users per arm to detect.

So the honest framing goes like this. The economics are favourable if the lift is above 0.25 points. The lift has to be measured, with the primary metric, the guardrails and the latency check of sections 05 to 11, because the larger model is also slower, at 60 tokens a second in the illustrative speeds. The decision follows the measurement.

This is the typical exam move in reverse. The larger model isn't always the expensive choice, and the smaller one isn't always the cheap one. The unit decides.
37676bf1c9:
The sensitivity panel names what to measure first. Doubling token prices raises cost per resolved conversation by 3.5 percent. Two points of resolution move it by 18 to 19 percent. Four more agent minutes per escalation move it by 47 percent.

So measure escalation handling time first, then resolution rate, then token prices. A team that spends its quarter negotiating token prices and trimming prompts, while escalation handling time goes unmeasured, is working on the shortest bar.

Chapter 1, section 12 makes the same point with the tornado of the ROI model. This is the version with the optimisation levers inside it.
2573d09216:
Cost optimisation without a meter is guesswork. The meter belongs in the client wrapper, not in a monthly spreadsheet.

The Messages API response carries a usage object with input and output tokens. When caching is on, it also carries the tokens written to and read from the cache (check the docs for exact field names). A wrapper computes the dollar cost from those counts and a price table held in configuration.

It records the cost with the tags that make every question in this chapter answerable: use case, segment, model, experiment arm, prompt version, cache hit, outcome. Chapter 10, Part 6 builds the attribution pipeline. This is its leaf.
7975870c7b:
Two rules keep the meter useful.

Keep the tag cardinality bounded. Segment, model, arm and prompt version are tens of values. Customer ID is millions, and it doesn't belong on a metric. It belongs in the trace and the per-tenant aggregate (chapter 10, Part 6).

And compute cost per outcome in the query layer, by dividing the cost counter by the outcome counter for the same tags. Then the dashboard that shows spend also shows spend per resolved conversation. The alert fires on drift in the ratio, not on the raw bill, which rises with healthy volume.
b3506ad8a5: Every row has the same shape. Neither option is wrong in general, and the stated numbers choose between them. Sometimes an exam scenario omits the number the choice depends on: the rate per prefix, the unit of the outcome, the percentile in the SLA. Then the right answer is often the one that goes and gets it.
e7f4231059: A before-and-after comparison confuses the change with everything else that changed that week: the campaign, the billing cycle, a competitor's outage, the weather in the region. The fix is a concurrent control arm for decisions. For diagnosis, use the mix-versus-rate decomposition of section 15. A before-and-after number is fine as a trigger for investigation, and never as a result.
2da5621f8a: Each scenario follows the same method. Name the primary requirement and the hard constraints. Write down what each option would cost or risk, with numbers. Eliminate options that violate a constraint. Then choose the simplest option the evidence supports. The wrong answers are written the way they appear on an exam: plausibly.
a90d9edd21:
Answer: C. The overall guardrail upper bound (+1.27) exceeds the registered margin (+1.0), so non-inferiority is not demonstrated. The segment-level harm in roaming breaches a per-segment requirement.

A fails the registration. B is a post-hoc rescue: extending changes the plan, and the problem isn't the width of the overall interval. D changes the model and the prompt in the same step, so a win couldn't be attributed, and it assumes a cause nobody has diagnosed.

C uses the structure. Segments are the decision units, and a partial rollout is a valid result.
a1bb84c125:
Answer: B. A violates the roaming requirement, and the per-segment rule is literal. D saves less and also fails roaming in the example (0.934). C doesn't reach the 60 percent target, and a discount is not a design.

B applies the levers in order of risk. The first (caching) can't change an output. The next two are measured trims. The model change is limited to the segment whose evidence clears the gate.

B also overshoots the target (79 versus 60 percent). That leaves room to spend on safety margin, or on a larger evaluation set for the next segment.
bbbc4cb44d:
Answer: shorten the output and parallelise. Streaming changes when the first token appears; it takes the first-token p95 from 9.7 to 2.3 seconds in example 16. It leaves the completion p95 where it was, and a parser that needs the whole object gets no benefit.

Decode time dominates. 650 tokens at 80 per second is about 8 seconds, and cutting the output moves the p95 from 15.2 to 9.7 seconds in the example. Parallel calls remove another 0.8 seconds. Both changes need the per-segment quality gate before they're kept.

The structure of the answer: identify which term the SLA names, find the lever that removes that term, and check that the lever doesn't break another constraint.
f1eecdfa72:
Answer: confirm, check the mix, then bisect with statistical verdicts and ablate.

  1. Confirm the drop with an interval, and check that the grader didn't change.
  2. Decompose by segment and input features to see whether the mix moved.
  3. Bisect the twelve changes on a stratified regression set: four builds instead of twelve, with grey verdicts getting more cases.
  4. Revert the culprit from head and confirm. If the head is still bad, bisect again. Finally, do a one-at-a-time ablation to catch an interaction.

In example 10, two changes (a chunk size change and an index rebuild) were harmless alone and harmful together. The fix was to change either one.

A full rollback throws away the good changes, and some of the twelve were improvements. It also destroys the evidence about which change did it. And it leaves the problem to come back with the next index rebuild.
b8312a6da8:
Answer: it does not finish in a reasonable time; change the design. A one-point lift on a 70 percent base needs 32,647 users per arm (example 01). Plan change gets 10 percent of 3,000 users per arm per day, which is 300 a day. The test would take about 109 days. That's past any sensible window, and the product will have changed by then.

The options, in the order to consider them:

  • Raise the minimum detectable effect, if a larger lift is what pays for the change. +3 points needs 3,554 per arm, 12 days for plan change.
  • Analyse plan change with a wider interval, and say so in the registration.
  • Pool it with a similar segment, on stated grounds.
  • Keep plan change on control and ship to the segments that can be proved.
  • Run a shadow comparison with paired outcomes, which needs far fewer cases (section 09).

What isn't acceptable is a registration that promises a per-segment result the traffic can't supply, or an overall result that lets plan change ride along.
f612b15396: On a Monday the finance dashboard shows the inference bill running at more than double the previous week. Traffic is flat. Quality metrics haven't moved. Here's the diagnosis, step by step, following the order of questions from section 14.
451a4a5100:
1. Is it real? Cost per request, from the meter in section 23, went from $0.0119 to $0.0267 on the mid tier. Volume is the same: 30,000 conversations a day, 2.5 requests each. At 2.25 million requests a month that's $26,775 against $60,075, a rise of $33,300 or 124 percent. The numbers match the "cache lost" row of example 14: $0.0267 is the cost of config B with no cache read.

2. Did the mix move? No. The share of each segment is unchanged, and tokens out per request are flat.

3. Where is it? Everywhere, and by route. The cache read tokens counter dropped to zero on all four routes at the same minute on Thursday afternoon.

4. What changed? The change log has one release at that minute: prompt v16. It added a line at the top of the system prompt, "Current time: 2026-10-01T14:03Z", so the model could reason about business hours. That line is different on every request. A per-request token at the front of the prefix turns one shared prefix into a distinct prefix per request, and the hit rate is zero.
44ac7f7a6d:
The fix is not a longer time-to-live. It moves the timestamp below the cache breakpoint, into the user turn or after the last cached block, and leaves the policy text byte-identical.

The regression test hashes the cached portion of the assembled prompt for two different simulated requests, and asserts that the hashes are equal. It's the same check as the byte-identical test in chapter 5, section 24.

The alert is a daily hit rate per route against the break-even of 21.7 percent, with an expectation of 95 percent or more on the four main routes.

The process lesson is the one this chapter keeps coming back to. The prompt change went through an offline evaluation of quality, which passed. It didn't go through a cost-and-latency check on the assembled request. The shadow rung would have caught it on the first mirrored request. The quality evaluation was fine; the cost model just wasn't part of the gate.
d6e1a83764: Notice what the diagnosis didn't need: a model change, a prompt rewrite, a new vendor or a meeting. It needed one metered line per request, a change log joined by timestamp, and an arithmetic check against a table from the companion code. The same pattern solves latency regressions (chapter 10's Tuesday scenario) and quality regressions (sections 14 to 16).
